2.0mu\scriptscriptstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle{\bullet}{c}\hfil$\crcr}}}\rrparenthesis,E)
in
q
.

(2)

\lambda\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}.u
is a sub-term of
t
for every m-closure
{\bullet}{(\lambda\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}.u,E)}
in
q
.

Tuples are Not Sub-Terms.

Point 2 only concerns evaluated m-closures containing abstractions, and
not
evaluated tuples. Consider
t:=(\lambda x.\lambda y.\llparenthesis x,y\rrparenthesis)\llparenthesis\mathtt{I}\rrparenthesis\llparenthesis\delta\rrparenthesis\rightarrow_{\beta_{v}}(\lambda y.\llparenthesis\mathtt{I},y\rrparenthesis)\llparenthesis\delta\rrparenthesis\rightarrow_{\beta_{v}}\llparenthesis\mathtt{I},\delta\rrparenthesis
in
\lambda_{\mathtt{sou}}
and note that
\llparenthesis\mathtt{I},\delta\rrparenthesis
is
not
a sub-term of
t
.
The run of the Source TAM on
t
produces a m-closure
(\llparenthesis{\bullet}\mathtt{I},{\bullet}\delta\rrparenthesis,E)
for some
E
.
The leaves of the tree-structure of an evaluated tuple are abstractions (
\mathtt{I}
and
\delta
in the example), which are initial sub-terms, but they might be arranged in ways that were not present in the initial term.

A consequence of this fact is that when the Source TAM starts evaluating a non-empty tuple
\llparenthesis\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.},t_{n}\rrparenthesis
with transition
\leadsto_{{\circ}sea_{3}}
, by adding
\llparenthesis\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.},\downarrow\rrparenthesis
to the stack, it has to
allocate a new tuple
on the heap for
\llparenthesis\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.},\downarrow\rrparenthesis
(which has a cost, discussed below). This never happens in absence of tuples, that is, in the LAM of Fig.
7
. More precisely, the LAM does not copy any code, but it has to allocate new pointers to local environments, when they are extended by
\leadsto_{\beta_{v}}
.

Step 1 of the Recipe: Number of Transitions and Overhead Measure

For establishing a bound on overhead transitions, we first factor some of them (
\leadsto_{{\bullet}sea_{1,3}}
) out by simply noticing that they are enabled and thus bound by some others (
\leadsto_{{\circ}sea_{1,3}}
). Actually, the same is true also for the principal transition
\leadsto_{{\bullet}\pi}
, bounded by
\leadsto_{{\circ}sea_{2}}
.

{toappendix}

Lemma 11.2 (Transition match).

Let
r
be a Source TAM run. Then
|r|_{\pi,{\bullet}sea_{1,3}}\leq|r|_{{\circ}sea_{1,2,3}}
.

For the other transitions, we use a measure
|\cdot|_{oh}
, defined in Fig.
11
together with the size
|t|
of
\lambda_{\mathtt{sou}}
terms, which we use to derive a bilinear bound on overhead/projection transitions (Prop.
11.4
).

​​​​
\begin{array}[]{rll@{\hspace{.3cm}} rll@{\hspace{.3cm}} rll}\lx@intercol\hfil\textsc{Size of $\lambda_{\mathtt{sou}}$ terms}\hfil\lx@intercol\\
|x|&\!\!\!:=&1\hfil\hskip 8.5359pt&|\lambda\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}.t|&\!\!\!:=&|t|+\lVert\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}\rVert+1\hfil\hskip 8.5359pt&|tu|&\!\!\!:=&|t|+|u|+1\\
|\pi_{i}t|&\!\!\!:=&|t|+1\hfil\hskip 8.5359pt&\lx@intercol\hfil|\llparenthesis t_{1},\dots,t_{n}\rrparenthesis|:=n+\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}|t_{i}|\hfil\lx@intercol\end{array}

\begin{array}[]{r@{\hspace{.2cm}} r@{\ }l@{\ }l@{\hspace{.35cm}} r@{\ }l@{\ }l@{\hspace{.35cm}} r@{\ }l@{\ }l}\lx@intercol\hfil\textsc{Overhead measure for the Source TAM }\hfil\lx@intercol\\
\textsc{\!\!\!\!\!\!\!Con. stack entries $S_{en}$}\hskip 5.69046pt&|{\bullet}{c}|_{oh}&:=&0\hfil\hskip 9.95863pt&|{\circ}{(t,E)}|_{oh}&:=&|t|\hfil\hskip 9.95863pt&|\pi_{i}|_{oh}&:=&0\\
\hskip 5.69046pt&\lx@intercol\hfil\!\!\!\!|(\llparenthesis{\circ}t_{1},\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.},{\circ}t_{n},\downarrow,\widetilde{\hbox{${\bullet}{c}$}}\rrparenthesis,E)|_{oh}:=n+\sum_{i=1}^{n}|t_{i}|_{oh}\hfil\lx@intercol\\
\textsc{Stacks}\hskip 5.69046pt&|\epsilon|_{oh}&:=&0\hfil\hskip 9.95863pt&\lx@intercol\hfil|S_{en}:S|_{oh}:=|S_{en}|_{oh}+|S|_{oh}\hfil\lx@intercol\\
\textsc{States}\hskip 5.69046pt&\lx@intercol\hfil|(\raisebox{1.0pt}{\scalebox{0.6}{\LEFTcircle}}c\mid S)|_{oh}:=|\raisebox{1.0pt}{\scalebox{0.6}{\LEFTcircle}}c|_{oh}+|S|_{oh}\hfil\lx@intercol\end{array}

Figure 11.
Size
|\cdot|
of
\lambda_{\mathtt{sou}}
terms and overhead measure
|\cdot|_{oh}
.

{toappendix}

Lemma 11.3 (Overhead measure properties).

Let
t^{\circ}\leadsto_{\textup{\tiny STAM}}^{*}q
a Source TAM run and
q\leadsto_{a}q^{\prime}
.

(1)

if
a={\bullet}\beta_{v}
then
|q^{\prime}|_{oh}\leq|q|_{oh}+|t|
;

(2)

if
a\in\{{\circ}sub,{\circ}sea_{1-5},{\bullet}sea_{6}\}
then
|q^{\prime}|_{oh}<|q|_{oh}
;

(3)

if
a\in\{{\bullet}sea_{1,3},{\bullet}\pi\}
then
|q^{\prime}|_{oh}=|q|_{oh}
.

{toappendix}

Proposition 11.4 (Bilinear bound on the number of transitions).

Let
t\!\in\!\lambda_{\mathtt{sou}}
be closed.
If
r\colon\!t^{\circ}\!\leadsto_{\textup{\tiny STAM}}^{*}\!q
then
|r|\!\in\!{\mathcal{O}}\big((|r|_{\beta_{v}}\!\!+\!1)\!\cdot\!|t|\big)
.

Tuples Raise the Overhead.

Prop.
11.4
shows that projection transitions are also bi-linear.
In
Section

10
, we mentioned that, without tuples, the bound improves to
{\mathcal{O}}(|r|_{\beta_{v}})
if one considers complete runs (that is, runs ending on values). With tuples, there is no such improvement. Indeed, even just checking that the initial term is actually a value
v
takes time
{\mathcal{O}}(|v|)
with tuples: if
v
is a tree of tuples, the Source TAM has to visit the tree and check that all the leaves are abstractions; in absence of tuples the check instead costs
{\mathcal{O}}(1)
.

Step 2 of the Recipe: Cost of Single Transitions

To obtain fine bounds with respect to the initial term, we introduce the notions of width and height of a term
t
, both bounded by the size
|t|
of
t
.

Definition 11.5 (Width, height).

The
width

\mathtt{wd}(t)\in\mathbb{N}
of
t\in\lambda_{\mathtt{sou}}
is the maximum length of a tuple or of a sequence of variables in
t
. The
height

\mathtt{hg}(t)\in\mathbb{N}
of
t\in\lambda_{\mathtt{sou}}
is the maximum number of bound variables of
t
in the scope of which a sub-term of
t
is contained.

As discussed after
Lemma

11.1
,
\leadsto_{{\circ}sea_{3}}
has to allocate a new tuple, thus its cost seems to depend on
\mathtt{wd}(t)
, and similarly for
\leadsto_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}
.
However, the price related to tuples can be considered as absorbed by the cost of search (by changing the multiplicative constant), since the new tuple of
\leadsto_{{\circ}sea_{3}}
is then traversed, if the run is long enough, and the one of
\leadsto_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}
was traversed before the transition.
Therefore, if we consider
complete
runs (i.e. ending on final states),
\leadsto_{{\circ}sea_{3}}
and
\leadsto_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}
have
amortized
cost independent of
\mathtt{wd}(t)
.

Transitions
{\bullet}sea_{1}
,
{\bullet}sea_{3}
, and
{\bullet}sea_{6}
duplicate
E
, the length of which is bound by
\mathtt{hg}(t)
. With flat environments, this costs
{\mathcal{O}}(\mathtt{hg}(t))
. Transition
\leadsto_{{\circ}sub}
has to look-up the environment, the cost of which is
{\mathcal{O}}(\mathtt{hg}(t))
. De Bruijn indices or an ordered domain of names might improve the cost of look-up, but at no overall advantage, because of the dominating cost of duplicating environments for
{\bullet}sea_{1}
,
{\bullet}sea_{3}
, and
{\bullet}sea_{6}
. All other transitions have constant cost, assuming that accessing the
i
-th component of a tuple (needed for
\leadsto_{{\bullet}\pi}
) takes constant time. The next proposition sums it up.

Proposition 11.6 (Cost of single transitions).

Let
r:t^{\circ}\leadsto_{\textup{\tiny STAM}}^{*}q
be a complete Source TAM run. A transition
\leadsto_{a}
of
r
has cost
{\mathcal{O}}(\mathtt{hg}(t))
if
a\in\{{\bullet}sea_{1},{\bullet}sea_{3},{\bullet}sea_{6},{\circ}sub\}
, and
{\mathcal{O}}(1)
otherwise.

Step 3 of the Recipe: Total Complexity

By simply multiplying the number of single transitions (Proposition
11.4
) for their cost (Proposition
11.6
), we obtain the complexity of the Source TAM.

{toappendix}

Theorem 11.7.

Let
t\in\lambda_{\mathtt{sou}}
be closed and
r:t^{\circ}\leadsto_{\textup{\tiny STAM}}^{*}q
be a complete Source TAM run. Then,
r
can be implemented on RAMs in time
{\mathcal{O}}\big((|r|_{\beta_{v}}+1)\cdot|t|\cdot\mathtt{hg}(t)\big)
.

If one flattens
\mathtt{hg}(t)
as
|t|
, the complexity of the Source TAM is
{\mathcal{O}}\big((|r|_{\beta_{v}}+1)\cdot|t|^{2}\big)
, that is, quadratic in
|t|
, while in absence of tuples—that is, for the LAM—it is linear in
|t|
.

12.
Part 3: Complexity of the Target TAM, or, Closure Conversion Preserves the Overhead

In this section, we adapt the time complexity analysis of the Source TAM to an analysis of the Target TAM (skipping the less efficient Int TAM), and then connect source and target by considering the impact of closure conversion on the given analysis.

The Target TAM has a sub-term invariant, expressed compactly thanks to our flags. In particular the part about abstractions of the sub-term invariant for the Source TAM (Lemma
11.1
) is here captured by having flagged the body of unevaluated closures with
{\circ}
.

{toappendix}

Lemma 12.1 (Sub-term invariant).

Let
q
be a Target TAM reachable state from the initial state
t^{\circ}
.
Then
u
is a sub-term of
t
for every non-evaluated term
{\circ}u
in
q
.

Step 1: Number of (Overhead) Transitions

The bound on the number of (overhead) transitions is obtained following the same reasoning used for the Source TAM. The new transition
\leadsto_{{\bullet}sea_{7}}
is part of the transitions that are factored out, since each
\leadsto_{{\bullet}sea_{7}}
transition is enabled by a
\leadsto_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}
transition, which adds an entry to the activation stack. We also use an overhead measure (in
Appendix

J
) which is a direct adaptation to the Target TAM of the one given for the Source TAM. Note indeed that the measure ignores environments, which are the main difference between the two machines.

{toappendix}

Proposition 12.2.

Let
t\in\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
be closed.
If
r\colon t^{\circ}\leadsto_{\textup{\tiny TTAM}}^{*}q
then
|r|\in{\mathcal{O}}\big((|r|_{\beta_{v}}+1)\cdot|t|\big)
.

Step 2: Cost of Single Transitions

For all transitions of the Target TAM but
\leadsto_{{\circ}sub_{v}}
,
\leadsto_{{\circ}sub_{c}}
, and
\leadsto_{{\bullet}sea_{7}}
the cost is the same.
For
\leadsto_{{\circ}sub_{v}}
, the cost is now
{\mathcal{O}}(1)
since tupled environments have
{\mathcal{O}}(1)
access time via indices (in the Int TAM its cost is instead
{\mathcal{O}}(\mathtt{hg}(t))
).

For the new transition
\leadsto_{{\circ}sub_{c}}
,
{\mathcal{O}}(\mathtt{wd}(t))
look-ups in the environment are needed.
Because of tupled environments, each look-up costs
{\mathcal{O}}(1)
. Thus, the cost seems to depend on
\mathtt{wd}(t)
, but—reasoning as for
\leadsto_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}
and
\leadsto_{{\circ}sea_{3}}
in
Section

11
—one can amortize it with the cost of search in complete runs. That is, we shall consider
\leadsto_{{\circ}sub_{c}}
to have constant cost. The new transition
\leadsto_{{\bullet}sea_{7}}
has constant cost as well.
Summing up, we get
one of the insights mentioned in the introduction: the amortized cost of all single transitions is
{\mathcal{O}}(1)
.

Proposition 12.3 (Cost of single transitions).

Let
r:t^{\circ}\leadsto_{\textup{\tiny TTAM}}^{*}q
be a complete Target TAM run. Every transition of
r
costs
{\mathcal{O}}(1)
.

Step 3: Total Complexity

Multiplying the number of single transitions (Prop.
12.2
) for their cost (Prop.
12.3
), we obtain the time complexity of the Target TAM, which seem better than for the Source TAM. After the theorem we discuss why it is not
necessarily so
.

Theorem 12.4.

Let
t\in\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
be closed and
r:t^{\circ}\leadsto_{\textup{\tiny TTAM}}^{*}q
be a complete Target TAM run. Then,
r
can be implemented on RAMs in time
{\mathcal{O}}\big((|r|_{\beta_{v}}+1)\cdot|t|\big)
.

Factoring in the Size Growth of Wrapping

To complete the analysis, take into account that the term
t\in\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
on which the Target TAM is run is meant to be the closure conversion (that is, wrapping + name elimination) of a term
u\in\lambda_{\mathtt{sou}}
. While name elimination does not affect the size of terms, wrapping
\underline{\cdot}
does (proof in
Appendix

J
).

{toappendix}

Lemma 12.5 (Wrapping size growth bound).

(1)

If
t\in\lambda_{\mathtt{sou}}
then
|\underline{t}|\in{\mathcal{O}}(\mathtt{hg}(t)\cdot|t|)
.

(2)

There are families of terms
\{t_{n}\}_{n\in\mathbb{N}}
for which
\mathtt{hg}(t_{n})=\Theta(|t_{n}|)
, so that
|\underline{t_{n}}|\in\Theta(|t_{n}|^{2})
.

We can now instantiate the bounds for running the Target TAM on the closure conversion of a
\lambda_{\mathtt{sou}}
term, obtained by substituting the bounds in Lemma
12.5
.2 in Theorem
12.4
. We end up obtaining the same complexity as for the Source TAM (Theorem
11.7
), despite the bound here being the outcome of a different reasoning.

Theorem 12.6.

Let
t\in\lambda_{\mathtt{sou}}
be closed and
r:(\hbox{\pagecolor{LightGray}$\underline{t}$}^{\footnotesize\epsilon,\epsilon})^{\circ}\leadsto_{\textup{\tiny TTAM}}^{*}q
be a complete Target TAM run. Then,
r
can be implemented on RAMs in time
{\mathcal{O}}\big((|r|_{\beta_{v}}+1)\cdot|t|\cdot\mathtt{hg}(t)\big)
.

13.
Related Work and Conclusions

Related work.

The seminal work of
Minamide et al. 1996
uses existential types to type closure conversion, and other works study the effect of closure conversion on types, as well as conversion towards typed target languages
(
Morrisett and Harper 1997
;
Ahmed and Blume 2008
;
Bowman and Ahmed 2018
)
.
This line of work explores the use of types in compilation which can span the entire compiler stack, from
\lambda
-calculus to (typed) assembly
(
Morrisett et al. 1999
)
.

Appel and co-authors have studied closure conversion, its efficient variants, and its
space safety

(
Appel and Jim 1989
;
Shao and Appel 1994
;
Shao and Appel 2000
;
Paraskevopoulou and Appel 2019
)
.
Unlike them, we address a direct style
\lambda
-calculus, without relying on a CPS. We are however inspired by
(
Paraskevopoulou and Appel 2019
)
in studying flat environments, also known as
flat closures
. Optimizations of flat closures are studied in
(
Keep et al. 2012
)
.

Closure conversion of only some abstractions, and of only some of their free variables is studied by
Wand and Steckler 1994
. Closure conversion has also been studied in relation to graphical languages
(
Schweimeier and Jeffrey 1999
)
,
non-strict languages
(
Sullivan et al. 2021
)
, formalizations
(
Chlipala 2010
;
Wang and Nadathur 2016
)
, extended to mutable state by
Mates et al. 2019
and to a type-preserving transformation for dependent types by
Bowman and Ahmed 2018
.

Many of the cited works study various aspects of the efficiency of closure conversion.
As said in the introduction, our concerns here are orthogonal, as we are rather interested in the asymptotic overhead of the machines with respect to flat closure conversion.

Sullivan et al. 2023
study a call-by-push-value
\lambda
-calculus where converted and non-converted functions live together, considering also an abstract machine. They do not study the complexity of the machine, nor the new notions of environments studied here.

For abstract machines, we follow Accattoli and co-authors, see for instance
(
Accattoli et al. 2014
;
Accattoli and Guerrieri 2019
;
Accattoli et al. 2019
)
. Another framework is
(
Felleisen et al. 2009
)
.

Work orthogonal to our concerns is the
derivation
of abstract machines using closure conversion as a step in the process, along with CPS transformation and defunctionalization
(
Ager et al. 2003
)
.

Conclusions.

We study the relationship between closure conversion and abstract machines in probably the simplest possible setting, an extension with tuples of Plotkin’s untyped call-by-value
\lambda
-calculus, and with respect to the simple notion of flat environments.
Our starting point is to decompose closure conversion in two sub-transformations, dubbed
wrapping
and
name elimination
, turning the source calculus into a target calculus, via
an intermediate one.

Each calculus is then paired with a variant of the
tupled abstract machine
(TAM). The Source TAM has machine-closures and local environments, while the Int TAM and the Target TAM have forms of converted closures. Moreover, they exploit the invariants enforced by the transformations, adopting new, better behaved forms of environments, namely
stackable
and
tupled environments
.

We give proof of correctness—under the form of termination-preserving strong bisimulations—for wrapping and name elimination, as well as implementation theorems for every machine with respect to its associated calculus. In particular, the proof technique for the correctness of closure conversion is new and simple.

Lastly, we study the time complexity of the abstract machines, showing that flat closure conversion reshuffles the costs, lowering the dependency on the initial term, while at the same time increasing the size of the initial term, ending up with the same complexity.

Appendix

There is a section of the Appendix for every section of the paper, containing the omitted proofs plus, possibly, some auxiliary notions.

\gettoappendix

l:intermediate-harmony

Proof.

If
t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{int}}u
, the fact that
u
is closed and clash-free follows from the hypothesis on
t
.
Let us prove, by induction on
t
, that
t
is a value or
t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{int}}u
for some
u\in\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
. Cases:

•

Variable
: impossible, because
t
is closed.

•

Closures
: then
t=\llbracket\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}};\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}.s|b\rrbracket
does not reduce and it is a value.

•

Projection
, that is,
t=\pi_{i}u
.
By
i.h.
,
u
is either a value or it reduces. Two cases:

–

u
is a value
. By clash-freeness, it must be a tuple
u=\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\mkern 2.0mu\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\displaystyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\hfil\displaystyle v\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\mkern 2.0mu\textstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\textstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\hfil\textstyle v\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\mkern 2.0mu\scriptstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\scriptstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\hfil\scriptstyle v\hfil$\crcr}}}{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\mkern 2.0mu\scriptscriptstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle\mkern 0.0mu\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraita}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraita}$}}}\mkern 0.0mu$}}{\hfill}\mkern-1.5mu\fldr$\crcr\kern-0.3pt\cr$\hfil\scriptscriptstyle v\hfil$\crcr}}}
of length
\geq i
. Therefore,

t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{i}\pi}v_{i}
.

–

u
reduces
. Then
t
reduces, because
\pi_{i}\langle\cdot\rangle
is an evaluation context.

•

Tuple
, that is,
t=\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\mkern 2.0mu\displaystyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\displaystyle\mkern 2.0mu\textstyle\mathrel{\mathchoice{{}\hbox{$\displaystyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\textstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}{{}\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\montraitd}$}}}\mkern-1.5mu\leaders{\hbox{$\textstyle\mkern \gettoappendix

l:lali-properties

Proof.

Straightforward inductions.
∎

Lemma B.5 (Basic properties of the reverse translation).

The following properties hold with respect to well-formed
\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
terms and evaluation contexts.

(1)

Values
: if
v\in\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
then
\lceil v\rceil
is a value of
\lambda_{\mathtt{sou}}
.

(2)

Evaluation contexts
: if
C\in\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
then
\lceil C\rceil
is an evaluation context of
\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
.

(3)

Root clashes
: if
t\in\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
is a root clash then
\lceil t\rceil
is a root clash of
\lambda_{\mathtt{sou}}
.

Proof.

The first two points are straightforward, the third is a simple unfolding of the definitions.∎

(2)

We prove the two implications separately.

•

t

\rightarrow_{\mathtt{int}}
-normal implies
\lceil t\rceil

\rightarrow_{\mathtt{sou}}
-normal
. By contradiction, suppose that
\lceil t\rceil=C\langle u\rangle
with
u
source root redex, so that
\lceil t\rceil
is not normal. We show that then
t=C^{\prime}\langle u^{\prime}\rangle
such that
\lceil C^{\prime}\rceil=C
,
\lceil u^{\prime}\rceil=u
, and
u^{\prime}
is an intermediate root redex. The proof is by induction on
C
. The base case is the crucial one, since it maps back source root redexes to intermediate root redexes. We give the crucial case, also showing the need of the closure hypothesis.

The inductive cases all follows from the
i.h.
and the fact that each case of
C
matches one and only one case for
C^{\prime}
, satisfying the statement.

•

\lceil t\rceil

\rightarrow_{\mathtt{sou}}
-normal implies
t

\rightarrow_{\mathtt{int}}
-normal
. By contradiction, assume that
t
is not
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{int}}
-normal. Then,
t
reduces and by projection (Point 1)
\lceil t\rceil
reduces. Absurd.

(3)

Note that if
t
is
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{int}}
-normal then, by the halt property (Point 2)
\lceil t\rceil
is
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{sou}}
-normal, against hypotheses. Then
t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{int}}s
for some
s
. By projection (Point 1),
\lceil t\rceil\rightarrow_{\mathtt{sou}}\lceil s\rceil
and it is the same kind of step than on
\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
. Since
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{sou}}
is deterministic (Lemma
A.2
),
\lceil s\rceil=u
.

(4)

Straightforward induction on
u
.
∎

\gettoappendix

cor:step-preservation

Proof.

By induction on
k
. If
k=0
then
t=u
;
taking
s:=\underline{t}
, the inverse property gives
\lceil s\rceil=\lceil\underline{t}\rceil=t=u
.
For
k>0
, one has
t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{sou}}^{k-1}u^{\prime}\rightarrow_{\mathtt{sou}}u
. By
i.h.
,
\underline{t}\rightarrow_{\mathtt{int}}^{k-1}s^{\prime}
with
\lceil s^{\prime}\rceil=u^{\prime}
, so
\lceil s^{\prime}\rceil\rightarrow_{\mathtt{sou}}u
;
by reflection
s^{\prime}\rightarrow_{\mathtt{int}}s
for some
s
such that
\lceil s\rceil=u
.
∎

Contextual closure

t\mapsto_{a}u

C\langle t\rangle\rightarrow_{a}C\langle u\rangle

for

\begin{array}[]{c}\textsc{Notation}\\
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{tar}}\ \ :=\ \ \rightarrow_{\mathtt{t}\beta_{v}}\cup\rightarrow_{\mathtt{t}\pi}\end{array}

Figure 12.
The target calculus
\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
.

In this section, we extend the outline of the target calculus
\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
and of name elimination given in Sect.
5
(the notions introduced there are not repeated here), giving more definitions as well as all the properties and proofs. The definition of
\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
in Fig.
12
adds the rewriting rules (and the notion of substitution they rely upon) to the grammars already given in Sect.
5
. The next paragraphs explain the involved concepts.

Projecting Substitution.

The elimination of names rises a slight technical issue in mapping steps from
\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
to
\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
, because it commutes with meta-level substitutions only
up to projections
. The replacement in
\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
of a variable
x
by a value
v\in\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
indeed is simulated in
\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
by:

To circumvent this issue, we define an ad-hoc notion of
projecting substitution
for the target calculus that performs the projections
on-the-fly
, that is, while substituting. Moreover, as for
\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
we define it as a simultaneous projecting substitution on both
\mathtt{w}
and
\mathtt{s}
.

In the next definition,
\lVert t\rVert_{\mathtt{w}}
and
\lVert t\rVert_{\mathtt{s}}
are the wrapped and source norms defined in Fig.
12
. They are extended to evaluation contexts as expected.

Definition C.1 (Well-formed closures/terms).

A closure
\llbracket t|b\rrbracket_{n,m}
is
well-formed
if
\lVert t\rVert_{\mathtt{w}}\leq n
,
\lVert t\rVert_{\mathtt{s}}\leq m
, and
\lVert b\rVert=n
.
Terms
t\in\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
and evaluation contexts
C\in\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
are
well-formed
if all their closures are well-formed.

Operational Semantics

The rewriting rules of
\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
(in Fig.
12
) are as those of
\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
up to the different notion of substitution in
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{t}\beta_{v}}
.

Definition C.3 (Clashes).

A well-formed term
t\in\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
is a
clash
if it has shape
C\langle u\rangle
where
u
has one of the following forms, called a
root clash
:

•

Clashing projection
:
t=\pi_{i}v
and (
v
is not a tuple or it is but
\lVert v\rVert<i
);

•

Clashing closure
:
t=\llbracket u|b\rrbracket_{n,m}v_{2}
and (
v_{2}
is not a tuple or it is but
m\neq\lVert\mathchoice{\vbox{\halign{#\cr\kern-0.7pt\cr$\mkern We say that
t\in\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
is
good
if it is well-formed and clash-free.

Lemma C.4 (Determinism).

Let
t\in\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
. If
t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{tar}}u
and
t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{tar}}s
then
u=s
and
t
is not a value.

Proof.

By induction on
t
.
∎

Lemma C.5 (Harmony for
\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
).

Let
t\in\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
be closed and good. Then either
t
is a value or
t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{tar}}u
for some closed good
u\in\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
.

Proof.

If
t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{tar}}u
, the fact that
u
is closed and clash-free follows from the hypothesis on
t
.
Let us prove, by induction on
t
, that
t
is a value or
t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{tar}}u
for some well-formed

. Cases:

•

Projected variable
: impossible, because
t
is closed.

•

Closures
: then

does not reduce and it is a value.

•

Projection

is an evaluation context.
∎

Figure 13.
Definition of the translation
\hbox{\pagecolor{LightGray}$t$}^{\footnotesize\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}:\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}\rightarrow\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
and the reverse translation
\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$t$}_{\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}:\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}\rightarrow\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
.

Translation.

The
name elimination
translation in Fig.
13
takes a well-formed and possibly open term
t\in\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
and two sequences of variables
\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}}\#\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}
, the sequence of
wrapped
variables
\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}}
and the sequence of
source
variables
\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}
, which together cover the free variables of
t
, that is,
\mathtt{fv}(t)\subseteq\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}}\#\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}
. We write
\hbox{\pagecolor{LightGray}$t$}^{\footnotesize\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}
for the translation of
t
with respect to the sequences
\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}}
and
\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}
.

Lemma C.6 (Basic properties of name elimination).

Let
\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}}
and
\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}
be two disjoint sequences of variables.

(1)

Values
: if
v\in\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
then
\hbox{\pagecolor{LightGray}$v$}^{\footnotesize\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}
is a value of
\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
.

(2)

Evaluation contexts
: if
C\in\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
then
\hbox{\pagecolor{LightGray}$C$}^{\footnotesize\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}
is an evaluation context of
\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
.

Proof.

(1)

Straightforward induction on
v
.

(2)

Straightforward induction on
C
, using the first point for the productions for evaluation contexts that involve values. ∎

The name elimination translation is a termination-preserving strong bisimulation between
\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
and
\lambda_{\mathtt{sou}}
as stated by Theorem
C.8
below, which is proved using the commutation of the substitution of
\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
with the translation of the next proposition. The theorem mimics the one relating
\lambda_{\mathtt{sou}}
and
\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
(Theorem
4.5
), but the statement is stronger as it does not need the closure hypothesis.

Theorem C.8 (Intermediate-target termination-preserving strong bisimulation).

Let
t\in\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
be well-formed and such that
\mathtt{fv}(t)\subseteq\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}}\#\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}
.

(1)

Projection
: if
t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{i}\beta_{v}}u
then
\hbox{\pagecolor{LightGray}$t$}^{\footnotesize\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}\rightarrow_{\mathtt{t}\beta_{v}}\hbox{\pagecolor{LightGray}$u$}^{\footnotesize\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}
and if
t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{i}\pi}u
then
\hbox{\pagecolor{LightGray}$t$}^{\footnotesize\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}\rightarrow_{\mathtt{t}\pi}\hbox{\pagecolor{LightGray}$u$}^{\footnotesize\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}
.

(2)

Halt
:
t
is
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{int}}
-normal (resp. a value, resp. a clash) if and only if
\hbox{\pagecolor{LightGray}$t$}^{\footnotesize\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}
is
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{tar}}
-normal (resp. a value, resp. a clash).

(3)

Reflection
: if
\hbox{\pagecolor{LightGray}$t$}^{\footnotesize\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}\rightarrow_{\mathtt{t}\beta_{v}}u
then there exists
s
such that
t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{i}\beta_{v}}s
and
\hbox{\pagecolor{LightGray}$s$}^{\footnotesize\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}=u
, and if
\hbox{\pagecolor{LightGray}$t$}^{\footnotesize\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}\rightarrow_{\mathtt{t}\pi}u
then there exists
s
such that
t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{i}\pi}s
and
\hbox{\pagecolor{LightGray}$s$}^{\footnotesize\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}=u
.

We prove the two implications separately.

t

\rightarrow_{\mathtt{int}}
-normal implies
\hbox{\pagecolor{LightGray}$t$}^{\footnotesize\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}

\rightarrow_{\mathtt{tar}}
-normal
. It is easily seen that the elimination of names cannot create redexes, values, or clashes, as it only acts on variables, replacing them with variables. For redexes, it amounts to show that if
\hbox{\pagecolor{LightGray}$t$}^{\footnotesize\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}\rightarrow_{\mathtt{t}\beta_{v}}u
then
t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{i}\beta_{v}}s
(then
\hbox{\pagecolor{LightGray}$s$}^{\footnotesize\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}=u
follows by projection and determinism of
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{t}\beta_{v}}
) by induction on the target evaluation context for the
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{t}\beta_{v}}
step, and similarly for
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{t}\pi}
. The base case is a simple inspection of the redexes and the translation, the inductive cases follow from the
i.h.
and from the immediate fact that the translation reflects values (that is, if
\hbox{\pagecolor{LightGray}$t$}^{\footnotesize\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}
is a value of
\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
then
t
is a value of
\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
). The reasoning for clashes is analogous, and for values it holds by Lemma
C.6
.

\rightarrow_{\mathtt{tar}}
-normal implies
t

\rightarrow_{\mathtt{int}}
-normal
. By contradiction, assume that
t
is not
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{tar}}
-normal. Then,
t
reduces and by projection (Point 1)
\hbox{\pagecolor{LightGray}$t$}^{\footnotesize\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}

t

From Source to Target

The two obtained strong bisimulation theorems—namely Theorem
4.5
and Theorem
C.8
—do not compose, because the first one uses the reverse translation from
\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
to
\lambda_{\mathtt{sou}}
, while the second one uses the direct translation from
\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
to
\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
. To solve the issue, we need a reverse translation from
\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
to
\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
, which is smoothly obtained. Such reverse
naming
translation is defined in Fig.
13
. It takes a well-formed
t\in\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
and two sequences of variables
\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}}\#\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}
such that
\lVert\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}}\rVert\geq\lVert t\rVert_{\mathtt{w}}
and
\lVert\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}\rVert\geq\lVert t\rVert_{\mathtt{s}}
and uses them to give names to the indices of the projections. We write
\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$t$}_{\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}
for the translation of
t
with respect to the sequences
\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}}
and
\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}
. On closed terms, the translation is meant to be applied with empty parameter lists (as
\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$t$}_{\epsilon,\epsilon}
).

Unsurprisingly, naming is a termination-preserved strong bisimulation from the target calculus to the intermediate one, as stated by the theorem below. For its proof, we need the mirror image of some of the results proved for name elimination.

Lemma C.9 (Basic properties of naming).

Let
\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}}
and
\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}
be two suitable disjoint sequences of variables.

(1)

Values
: if
v\in\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
then
\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$v$}_{\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}
is a value of
\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
.

(2)

Evaluation contexts
: if
C\in\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
then
\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$C$}_{\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}
is an evaluation context of
\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
.

Proof.

Straightforward inductions.∎

for any

Proof.

Analogous to the proof of Proposition
C.7
.∎

The next auxiliary lemma is needed for the inverse property.

Lemma C.11.

Let
t\in\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
such that
\mathtt{fv}(t)\subseteq\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}}\#\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}
and let
\widetilde{\hbox{$z$}}
and
\widetilde{\hbox{$w$}}
be such that
\lVert\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}}\rVert=\lVert\widetilde{\hbox{$z$}}\rVert
and
\lVert\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}\rVert=\lVert\widetilde{\hbox{$w$}}\rVert
. Then
\hbox{\pagecolor{LightGray}$t$}^{\footnotesize\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}=\hbox{\pagecolor{LightGray}$t\{\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}};\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}{\shortleftarrow}\widetilde{\hbox{$z$}};\widetilde{\hbox{$w$}}\}$}^{\footnotesize\widetilde{\hbox{$z$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$w$}}}
.

Proof.

By induction on
t
.
∎

The next theorem is given in the special case of
t
closed because it is how it is applied in the final bisimulation theorem after it, but it could be more generally stated for open terms, as it is the case for name elimination (Theorem
C.8
).

Theorem C.12 (Target-intermediate termination-preserving strong bisimulation).

Let
t\in\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
be closed.

(1)

Projection
: if
t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{t}\beta_{v}}u
then
\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$t$}_{\epsilon,\epsilon}\rightarrow_{\mathtt{i}\beta_{v}}\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$u$}_{\epsilon,\epsilon}
and if
t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{t}\pi}u
then
\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$t$}_{\epsilon,\epsilon}\rightarrow_{\mathtt{i}\pi}\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$u$}_{\epsilon,\epsilon}
.

(2)

Halt
:
t
is
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{tar}}
-normal (resp. a value, resp. a clash) if and only if
\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$t$}_{\epsilon,\epsilon}
is
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{tar}}
-normal (resp. a value, resp. a clash).

(3)

Reflection
: if
\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$t$}_{\epsilon,\epsilon}\rightarrow_{\mathtt{i}\beta_{v}}u
then there exists
s
such that
t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{t}\beta_{v}}s
and
\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$s$}_{\epsilon,\epsilon}=u
, and if
\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$t$}_{\epsilon,\epsilon}\rightarrow_{\mathtt{i}\pi}u
then there exists
s
such that
t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{t}\pi}s
and
\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$s$}_{\epsilon,\epsilon}=u
.

(4)

Inverse
: let
t\in\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
such that
\mathtt{fv}(t)\subseteq\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}}\#\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}
. Then
\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$\hbox{\pagecolor{LightGray}$t$}^{\footnotesize\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}$}_{\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}},\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}}=_{\alpha}t
.

Proof.

The following theorem states that the reverse transformation
\lceil\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$t$}_{\epsilon,\epsilon}\rceil
of closure conversion (obtained by composing naming and unwrapping) is a termination-preserving strong bisimulation. It is our correctness result for closure conversion. The proof is obtained by simply composing the two bisimulations results for unwrapping (Theorem
4.5
) and naming (Theorem
C.12
).

Theorem C.13 (Target-source termination-preserving strong bisimulation).

Let
t\in\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
be closed.

(1)

Projection
: if
t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{t}\beta_{v}}u
then
\lceil\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$t$}_{\epsilon,\epsilon}\rceil\rightarrow_{\beta_{v}}\lceil\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$u$}_{\epsilon,\epsilon}\rceil
and if
t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{t}\pi}u
then
\lceil\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$t$}_{\epsilon,\epsilon}\rceil\rightarrow_{\pi}\lceil\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$u$}_{\epsilon,\epsilon}\rceil
.

(2)

Halt
:
t
is
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{tar}}
-normal if and only if
\lceil\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$t$}_{\epsilon,\epsilon}\rceil
is
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{sou}}
-normal.

(3)

Reflection
: if
\lceil\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$t$}_{\epsilon,\epsilon}\rceil\rightarrow_{\beta_{v}}u
then there exists
s
such that
t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{t}\beta_{v}}s
and
\lceil\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$s$}_{\epsilon,\epsilon}\rceil=u
, and if
\lceil\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$t$}_{\epsilon,\epsilon}\rceil\rightarrow_{\pi}u
then there exists
s
such that
t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{t}\pi}s
and
\lceil\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$s$}_{\epsilon,\epsilon}\rceil=u
.

(4)

Inverse
: if
u\in\lambda_{\mathtt{sou}}
then
\lceil\hbox{\pagecolor{DarkGray}$\hbox{\pagecolor{LightGray}$\underline{u}$}^{\footnotesize\epsilon,\epsilon}$}_{\epsilon,\epsilon}\rceil=u
.

Appendix D
Proofs and Auxiliary Notions of Sect.
6
(Preliminaries About Abstract Machines)

Lemma D.1 (One-step simulation).

Let
\mathtt{M}=(\mathtt{States},\leadsto,\cdot^{\circ},\underline{\cdot})
be a machine and
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{str}}
be a deterministic strategy forming an implementation system.
For any state
q
of
\mathtt{M}
, if
\underline{q}\rightarrow_{\mathtt{str}}u
is a step of label
l
then there is a state
q^{\prime}
of
\mathtt{M}
such that
q\leadsto_{oh}^{*}\leadsto_{pr}q^{\prime}
where the last transition has label
l
and
\underline{q^{\prime}}=u
.

Proof.

For any state
q
of
\mathtt{M}
, let
\mathtt{nf}_{oh}(q)
be a normal form of
q
with respect to
\leadsto_{oh}
: such a state exists because overhead transitions terminate (by the overhead termination property of implementation systems).
Since
\leadsto_{oh}
is mapped on identities (by overhead transparency), one has
\underline{\mathtt{nf}_{oh}(q)}=\underline{q}
.
The hypothesis then becomes
\underline{q}=\underline{\mathtt{nf}_{oh}(q)}\rightarrow_{\mathtt{str}}u
. By the halt property,
\mathtt{nf}_{oh}(q)
cannot be a final state (successful or clash), otherwise
\underline{q}=\underline{\mathtt{nf}_{oh}(q)}
could not reduce. Since
\mathtt{nf}_{oh}(q)
is
\leadsto_{oh}
-normal, we have
\mathtt{nf}_{oh}(q)\leadsto_{pr}q^{\prime}
for some
q^{\prime}
. By principal projection,
\underline{\mathtt{nf}_{oh}(q)}\rightarrow_{\mathtt{str}}\underline{q^{\prime}}
, and the step and the transition have the same label. By determinism of
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{str}}
,
\underline{q^{\prime}}=u
.
∎

thm:abs-impl

Proof.

According to Definition
6.1
, given a term
t\in\lambda_{cal}
, we have to show that:

(1)

Runs to evaluations with
\beta
-matching
: for any
\mathtt{M}
-run

there exists a

\rightarrow_{\mathtt{str}}
-evaluation

such that
|e|_{l}=|r|_{l}
for every label

of steps in
\lambda_{cal}
. Additionally, if
q
is a successful state then
\underline{q}
is a
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{str}}
-normal form.

(2)

Evaluations to runs with
\beta
-matching
: for every
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{str}}
-evaluation
e:t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{str}}^{*}u
there exists a

\mathtt{M}
-run
r:t^{\circ}\leadsto_{\mathtt{M}}^{*}q
such that
\underline{q}=u
and
|e|_{l}=|r|_{l}
for every label
l
of steps in
\lambda_{cal}
. Additionally, if
u
is a
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{str}}
-normal form then there exists a successful state
q^{\prime}
such that
q\leadsto_{oh}^{*}q^{\prime}
.

Proof of Point
1

By induction on the number of principal transition
|r|_{pr}\in\mathbb{N}
in
r
.

If
|r|_{pr}=0
then
r\colon t^{\circ}\leadsto_{oh}^{*}q
and hence
\underline{t^{\circ}}=\underline{q}
by overhead transparency (Point
1
of Definition
6.2
).
Moreover,
t=\underline{t^{\circ}}
since read-back is the inverse of initialization on initial states, therefore the statement holds by taking the empty (i.e. without steps) evaluation
e
with starting (and end) term
t
.

Suppose
|r|_{pr}>0
: then,
r\colon t^{\circ}\leadsto_{\mathtt{M}}^{*}q
is the concatenation of a run
r^{\prime}\colon t^{\circ}\leadsto_{\mathtt{M}}^{*}q^{\prime}
followed by a run
r^{\prime\prime}\colon q^{\prime}\leadsto_{pr}q^{\prime\prime}\leadsto_{oh}^{*}q
.
By
i.h.
applied to
r^{\prime}
, there exists an evaluation
e^{\prime}\colon t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{str}}^{*}\underline{q^{\prime}}
with
|r^{\prime}|_{l}=|e^{\prime}|_{l}
.
By principal projection (Point
2
of Definition
6.2
) and overhead transparency (Point
1
of Definition
6.2
) applied to
r^{\prime\prime}
, one has
e^{\prime\prime}\colon\underline{q^{\prime}}\rightarrow_{\mathtt{str}}\underline{q^{\prime\prime}}=\underline{q}
for a
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{str}}
-step of the same label
l^{\prime}
as the transition
q^{\prime}\leadsto_{pr}q^{\prime\prime}
.
Therefore, the evaluation
e
defined as the concatenation of
e^{\prime}
and
e^{\prime\prime}
is such that
e\colon t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{str}}^{*}\underline{q}
Moreover:

•

|e|_{l^{\prime}}=|e^{\prime}|_{l^{\prime}}+|e^{\prime\prime}|_{l^{\prime}}=|r^{\prime}|_{l^{\prime}}+1=|r|_{l^{\prime}}
.

•

|e|_{l}=|e^{\prime}|_{l}+|e^{\prime\prime}|_{l}=|r^{\prime}|_{l}+0=|r|_{l}
for every label
l\neq l^{\prime}
.

If
q
is a successful state, by the halt property (Point
4
of Definition
6.2
)
\underline{q}
is a
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{str}}
-normal form.

Proof of Point
2

By induction on
|e|\in\mathbb{N}
.

If
|e|=0
then
t=u
.
Since read-back is the inverse of initialization on initial states, one has
\underline{t^{\circ}}=t
.
The statement holds by taking the empty (i.e. without transitions) run
r
with initial (and final) state
t^{\circ}
.

Suppose
|e|>0
: so,
e\colon t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{str}}^{*}u
is the concatenation of an evaluation
e^{\prime}\colon t\rightarrow_{\mathtt{str}}^{*}u^{\prime}
followed by the step
u^{\prime}\rightarrow_{\mathtt{str}}u
.
By
i.h.
, there exists a
\mathtt{M}
-run
r^{\prime}\colon t^{\circ}\leadsto_{\mathtt{M}}^{*}q^{\prime}
such that
\underline{q^{\prime}}=u^{\prime}
and
|e^{\prime}|_{l}=|r^{\prime}|_{l}
(the state
q^{\prime}
here is not the one of the
additionally
part of the statement).
By one-step simulation (Lemma
D.1
, since
\underline{q^{\prime}}\rightarrow_{\mathtt{str}}u
and
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{str}}
and
\mathtt{M}
form an implementation system), there is a state
q
of
\mathtt{M}
such that
q^{\prime}\leadsto_{oh}^{*}\leadsto_{pr}q
with its last transition having the same label
l^{\prime}
of the step
\underline{q^{\prime}}\rightarrow_{\mathtt{str}}u
, and such that
\underline{q}=u
.
Therefore, the run
r\colon t^{\circ}\leadsto_{\mathtt{M}}^{*}q^{\prime}\leadsto_{oh}^{*}\leadsto_{pr}q
is such that:

•

|r|_{l^{\prime}}=|r^{\prime}|_{l^{\prime}}+1=|e^{\prime}|_{l^{\prime}}+1=|e|_{l^{\prime}}
;

•

|r|_{l}=|r^{\prime}|_{l}=|e^{\prime}|_{l}=|e|_{l}
; for every label
l\neq l^{\prime}
.

If
u
is a
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{str}}
-normal form, then consider
\mathtt{nf}_{oh}(q)
. If
\mathtt{nf}_{oh}(q)
is not final, then by overhead transparency
\underline{\mathtt{nf}_{oh}(q)}=\underline{q}=u
and by principal projection
u
is not
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{str}}
-normal, absurd. Then it is a final state. By the halt property,
\mathtt{nf}_{oh}(q)
is a successful state, providing the state
q^{\prime}
of the statement.
∎

Lemma E.2.

For every Source TAM flagged closure
\raisebox{1.0pt}{\scalebox{0.6}{\LEFTcircle}}c
,
\underline{\raisebox{1.0pt}{\scalebox{0.6}{\LEFTcircle}}c}
is a term. In particular:

(1)

If
\raisebox{1.0pt}{\scalebox{0.6}{\LEFTcircle}}c=\raisebox{1.0pt}{\scalebox{0.6}{\LEFTcircle}}(\lambda\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}.t,E)
, then
\underline{\raisebox{1.0pt}{\scalebox{0.6}{\LEFTcircle}}(\lambda\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}.t,E)}=\lambda x.\underline{(t,E)}
.

(2)

If
\raisebox{1.0pt}{\scalebox{0.6}{\LEFTcircle}}c=\raisebox{1.0pt}{\scalebox{0.6}{\LEFTcircle}}(tu,E)
, then
\underline{\raisebox{1.0pt}{\scalebox{0.6}{\LEFTcircle}}(tu,E)}=\underline{(t,E)}\,\underline{(u,E)}
.

(3)

If
\raisebox{1.0pt}{\scalebox{0.6}{\LEFTcircle}}c=\raisebox{1.0pt}{\scalebox{0.6}{\LEFTcircle}}(\pi_{i}t,E)
, then
\underline{\raisebox{1.0pt}{\scalebox{0.6}{\LEFTcircle}}(\pi_{i}t,E)}=\pi_{i}\underline{(t,E)}
.

(4)

If
\raisebox{1.0pt}{\scalebox{0.6}{\LEFTcircle}}c=\raisebox{1.0pt}{\scalebox{0.6}{\LEFTcircle}}(x,E)
and
x\in\mathtt{dom}(E)
, then
\underline{\raisebox{1.0pt}{\scalebox{0.6}{\LEFTcircle}}(x,E)}=\underline{E(x)}
.

Proof.

By induction on the length of the environment
E
.
∎

Proposition E.3 (Source implementation system).

The
\rightarrow_{\pi}
step is correct because
\underline{S}
is an evaluation context by the read back invariants (Lemma
7.2
).

(2)

(a)

({\circ}(tu,E)\mid S)\leadsto_{{\circ}sea_{1}}({\circ}(u,E)\mid{\circ}{(t,E)}:S)
.
Then,

\begin{array}[]{llll}\underline{({\circ}(tu,E)\mid S)}&=&\underline{S}\langle\underline{{\circ}(tu,E)}\rangle\\[5.0pt]
&=_{{L.\ref{l:TAM-decode-laxclosure}.\ref{p:TAM-decode-laxclosure-application}}}&\underline{S}\langle\underline{{\circ}{(t,E)}}\langle\underline{{\circ}(u,E)}\rangle\rangle\\[5.0pt]
&=&\underline{({\circ}(u,E)\mid{\circ}{(t,E)}:S)}.\end{array}

(b)

({\circ}(\pi_{i}t,E)\mid S)\leadsto_{{\circ}sea_{2}}({\circ}(t,E)\mid\pi_{i}:S)
. Then,

\begin{array}[]{llll}\underline{({\circ}(\pi_{i}t,E)\mid S)}&=\underline{S}\langle\underline{{\circ}(\pi_{i}t,E)}\rangle=_{{L.\ref{l:TAM-decode-laxclosure}.\ref{p:TAM-decode-laxclosure-projection}}}\underline{S}\langle\pi_{i}\underline{{\circ}(t,E)}\rangle=\underline{({\circ}(t,E)\mid\pi_{i}:S)}.\end{array}

(c)

({\circ}(\llparenthesis\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.},t_{n}\rrparenthesis,E)\mid S)\leadsto_{{\circ}sea_{3}}({\circ}(t_{n},E)\mid(\llparenthesis\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.},\downarrow\rrparenthesis,E):S)
with
n>0
. Then,

\begin{array}[]{llll}\underline{({\circ}(\llparenthesis\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.},t_{n}\rrparenthesis,E)\mid S)}&=&\underline{S}\langle\underline{{\circ}(\llparenthesis\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.},t_{n}\rrparenthesis,E)}\rangle\\[5.0pt]
&=&\underline{S}\langle\llparenthesis\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.},\underline{{\circ}(t_{n},E)}\rrparenthesis\rangle\\[5.0pt]
&=&\underline{({\circ}(t_{n},E)\mid(\llparenthesis\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.},\downarrow\rrparenthesis,E):S)}.\end{array}

(d)

({\circ}(\llparenthesis\rrparenthesis,E)\mid S)\leadsto_{{\circ}sea_{4}}({\bullet}(\llparenthesis\rrparenthesis,\epsilon)\mid S)
. Then,

\begin{array}[]{llll}\underline{({\circ}(\llparenthesis\rrparenthesis,E)\mid S)}&=\underline{S}\langle\underline{(\llparenthesis\rrparenthesis,E)}\rangle=\underline{({\bullet}(\llparenthesis\rrparenthesis,\epsilon)\mid S)}.\end{array}

(e)

({\circ}(\lambda\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}.t,E)\mid S)\leadsto_{{\circ}sea_{5}}({\bullet}(\lambda\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}.t,E)\mid S)
. Then,

\begin{array}[]{llll}\underline{({\circ}(\lambda\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}.t,E)\mid S)}&=\underline{S}\langle\underline{(\lambda\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}.t,E)}\rangle=\underline{({\bullet}(\lambda\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}.t,E)\mid S)}.\end{array}

(f)

({\circ}(x,E)\mid S)\leadsto_{sub}(E(x)\mid S)
. Then,

\begin{array}[]{llll}\underline{({\circ}(x,E)\mid S)}&=\underline{S}\langle\underline{{\circ}(x,E)}\rangle=_{{L.\ref{l:TAM-decode-laxclosure}.\ref{p:TAM-decode-laxclosure-variable}}}\underline{S}\langle\underline{E(x)}\rangle=\underline{(E(x)\mid S)}.\end{array}

(g)

({\bullet}{c}\mid{\circ}{(t,E)}:S)\leadsto_{{\bullet}sea_{1}}({\circ}(t,E)\mid{\bullet}{c}:S)
. Then,

\begin{array}[]{llll}\underline{({\bullet}{c}\mid{\circ}{(t,E)}:S)}&=\underline{S}\langle\underline{{\circ}(t,E)}\,\underline{{\bullet}{c}}\rangle=\underline{({\circ}(t,E)\mid{\bullet}{c}:S)}.\end{array}

(h)

({\bullet}{c}\mid(\llparenthesis\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.},t,\downarrow,\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.}\rrparenthesis,E):S)\leadsto_{{\bullet}sea_{6}}({\circ}(t,E)\mid(\llparenthesis\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.},\downarrow,{\bullet}{c},\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.}\rrparenthesis,E):S)
. Then,

\begin{array}[]{llll}\underline{({\bullet}{c}\mid(\llparenthesis\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.},t,\downarrow,\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.}\rrparenthesis,E):S)}&=\underline{S}\langle\llparenthesis\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.},(t,E),\underline{{\bullet}{c}},\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.}\rrparenthesis\rangle=\underline{({\circ}(t,E)\mid(\llparenthesis\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.},\downarrow,{\bullet}{c},\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.}\rrparenthesis,E):S)}.\end{array}

(i)

({\bullet}{c}\mid(\llparenthesis\downarrow,\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.}\rrparenthesis,E):S)\leadsto_{{\bullet}sea_{3}}(\llparenthesis{\bullet}{c},\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.}\rrparenthesis\mid S)
. Then,

\begin{array}[]{llll}\underline{({\bullet}{c}\mid(\llparenthesis\downarrow,\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.}\rrparenthesis,E):S)}&=\underline{S}\langle\llparenthesis\underline{{\bullet}{c}},\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.}\rrparenthesis\rangle=\underline{(\llparenthesis{\bullet}{c},\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.}\rrparenthesis\mid S)}.\end{array}

(3)

The proof of this point is omitted here, as it is a consequence of the complexity analysis of Sect.
11
, see Proposition
11.4
.

(4)

Let
(\raisebox{1.0pt}{\scalebox{0.6}{\LEFTcircle}}c,S)
be a final state. Two cases for
\raisebox{1.0pt}{\scalebox{0.6}{\LEFTcircle}}c
:

•

Non-evaluated closure

{\circ}{c}
. Then the only possibility is that
{\circ}{c}={\circ}{(x,E)}
with
x\notin\mathtt{dom}(E)
, but by the closure invariant (Lemma
7.1
) this is impossible.

•

Evaluated closure

{\bullet}{c}
. Then consider the stack
S
.

–

S
is empty
. Then
q
reads back to a value
\underline{({\bullet}{c}\mid\epsilon)}=\underline{{\bullet}{c}}
by the read back invariants (Lemma
7.2
.1), which by harmony (Lemma
3.2
) is a normal form.

–

S
has a non-evaluated closure
{\circ}{c}
on top
, that is,
S={\circ}{c}:S^{\prime}
. Then transition
\leadsto_{{\bullet}sea_{1}}
applies, and the state was not final, absurd.

–

S
has a tuple
(\llparenthesis\hbox to6.13336pt{.\hss.},t,\downarrow,\hbox to6.13336pt{.\hss.}\rrparenthesis,E)
on top
, that is,
S=(\llparenthesis\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.},t,\downarrow,\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.}\rrparenthesis,E):S^{\prime}
. Then transition
\leadsto_{{\bullet}sea_{6}}
applies, and the state was not final, absurd.

–

S
has a tuple
(\llparenthesis\downarrow,\hbox to6.13336pt{.\hss.}\rrparenthesis,E)
on top
, that is,
S=(\llparenthesis\downarrow,\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.}\rrparenthesis,E):S^{\prime}
. Then transition
\leadsto_{{\bullet}sea_{3}}
applies, and the state was not final, absurd.

–

S
has a closure
{\bullet}{c^{\prime}}
on top
, that is,
S={\bullet}{c^{\prime}}:S^{\prime}
. Cases of
{\bullet}{c}
:

*

{\bullet}{c}
is a tuple
. Then
q
is a clash state (clashing tuple) and its read back
\underline{q}=\underline{S^{\prime}}\langle\underline{{\bullet}{c}}\,\underline{{\bullet}{c^{\prime}}}\rangle
is the corresponding kind of term clash.

*

{\bullet}{c}
is an abstraction closure
{\bullet}{(\lambda\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}.t,E)}
. Two sub-cases.

·

{\bullet}{c^{\prime}}
is not a tuple
. Then
q
is a clash state (clashing abstraction with wrong argument) and its read back is the corresponding kind of term clash.

·

{\bullet}{c^{\prime}}
is a tuple
. Two sub-cases:

(a)

\lVert\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}\rVert\neq\lVert{\bullet}{c^{\prime}}\rVert
. Then
q
is a clash state (clashing abstraction with arity mismatch) and its read back is the corresponding kind of term clash.

(b)

\lVert\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}\rVert=\lVert{\bullet}{c^{\prime}}\rVert
. This case is impossible because then
q
can do a
\leadsto_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}
transition, which is absurd.

–

S
has a projection
\pi_{i}
on top
, that is,
S=\pi_{i}:S^{\prime}
. Cases of
{\bullet}{c}
:

*

{\bullet}{c}
is a tuple
. Two sub-cases.

·

\lVert\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}\rVert\neq\lVert{\bullet}{c^{\prime}}\rVert
. Then
q
is a clash state (clashing projection with arity mismatch) and its read back is the corresponding case of term clash.

·

\lVert\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}\rVert=\lVert{\bullet}{c^{\prime}}\rVert
. This case is impossible because then
q
can do a
\leadsto_{{\bullet}\pi}
transition, which is absurd.

*

{\bullet}{c}
is an abstraction closure
{\bullet}{(\lambda\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}.t,E)}
. Then
q
is a clash state (clashing projection with wrong argument) and its read back is the corresponding case of term clash.∎

by the abstract theorem Theorem

.∎

\gettoappendix

prop:LTAM-invariants

Proof.

(1)

By induction on the length of the execution ending on
q
. For the initial state, it follows from the requirement that compiled terms are prime (which is an extension of well-formed). For the inductive case, one considers each transition, and the statement for the target state immediately follows from the
i.h.
about the source state.

(2)

By induction on the length of the execution ending on
q
. For each transition, it immediately follows from the
i.h.
, but for
\leadsto_{{\circ}sub_{c}}
which needs the well-formedness invariant (Lemma
8.1
) to prove that
{\bullet}\llbracket\widetilde{\hbox{$y$}};\widetilde{\hbox{$x$}}.{\circ}t|{\bullet}{v}\rrbracket
is closed.

(3)

The two parts:

(a)

\mathtt{fv}(t)\cup\mathtt{fv}(S)\subseteq\mathtt{dom}(E)
;

(b)

\mathtt{fv}(S^{\prime})\subseteq\mathtt{dom}(E^{\prime})
for every entry
(S^{\prime},E^{\prime})
of the environment stack
A
.

are proved at the same time, by induction on the length of the execution ending on
q
. For most transitions, it immediately follows from the
i.h.
The relevant cases are (they show in particular that the two parts have to be proved simultaneously):

•

In
\leadsto_{{\circ}sub_{c}}
and
\leadsto_{{\circ}sub_{v}}
, we need the closed values invariant (Point 2) on the source state to prove part
a
about
E(x)
for the target state.

•

In
\leadsto_{{\bullet}sea_{7}}
, we need part
b
and the closed values invariant (Point 2) on the source state to prove part
a
for the target state.

•

In
\leadsto_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}
, we need part
a
on the source state to prove part
b
on the target state. Part
a
for the target state holds because of the well-formed invariant (Point 1).∎

\gettoappendix

l:LTAM-decoding-invariants

Proof.

For constructor stacks, we proceed by induction on
S
. Cases:

•

Empty

S=\epsilon
. Then
\underline{S}=\langle\cdot\rangle
is an evaluation context.

•

Projection

S=\pi_{i}:S^{\prime}
. Then
\underline{S}=\underline{S^{\prime}}\langle\pi_{i}\langle\cdot\rangle\rangle
. By
i.h.
,
\underline{S^{\prime}}
is an evaluation context. Note that
\pi_{i}\langle\cdot\rangle
is also an evaluation context. By the composition of evaluation contexts (Lemma
B.2
), so does
\underline{S}=\underline{S^{\prime}}\langle\pi_{i}\langle\cdot\rangle\rangle
.

•

Evaluated value

S=\underline{{\bullet}{v}:S^{\prime}}
. By
i.h.
,
\underline{S^{\prime}}
is an evaluation context. Note that
\langle\cdot\rangle\underline{{\bullet}v}
is also an evaluation context, because by Point 1
\underline{{\bullet}v}
is a value. By the composition of evaluation contexts (Lemma
B.2
), so does
\underline{S}=\underline{S^{\prime}}\langle\langle\cdot\rangle\underline{{\bullet}v}\rangle
.

•

Non-evaluated term

S=\underline{{\circ}{t}:S^{\prime}}
. By
i.h.
,
\underline{S^{\prime}}
is an evaluation context. Note that
t\langle\cdot\rangle
is also an evaluation context. By the composition of evaluation contexts (Lemma
B.2
), so does
Then
\underline{S}=\underline{S^{\prime}}\langle t\langle\cdot\rangle\rangle
.

•

Tuple

S=\llparenthesis t_{1},\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.},t_{n},\downarrow,{\bullet}v_{1},\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.},{\bullet}v_{m}\rrparenthesis:S^{\prime}
. By
i.h.
,
\underline{S^{\prime}}
is an evaluation context. Note that
\llparenthesis t_{1},\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.},t_{n},\langle\cdot\rangle,\underline{{\bullet}v_{1}},\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.},\underline{{\bullet}v_{m}}\rrparenthesis
also is an evaluation context, because by Point 1
\underline{{\bullet}v_{m}}
is a value. By the composition of evaluation contexts (Lemma
B.2
), so does
\underline{S}=\underline{S^{\prime}}\langle\llparenthesis t_{1},\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.},t_{n},\langle\cdot\rangle,\underline{{\bullet}v_{1}},\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.},\underline{{\bullet}v_{m}}\rrparenthesis\rangle
.

For activation stacks, we proceed by induction on
A
. Cases:

•

Empty

A=\epsilon
. Then
\underline{A}=\langle\cdot\rangle
is an evaluation context.

•

Non-empty

A=(S,E):A^{\prime}
. By
i.h.
,
\underline{A^{\prime}}
is an evaluation context. Since
\underline{S}
is an evaluation context by the point about constructor stacks,
\underline{S}\sigma_{E}
is an evaluation context. By the composition of evaluation contexts (Lemma
B.2
), so does
\underline{A}\langle\underline{S}\sigma_{E}\rangle
.∎

Proposition F.3 (Intermediate implementation system).

Let
q
be a Int TAM reachable state.

(1)

Principal project.
: for
a\in\{\beta_{v},\pi\}
, if
q\leadsto_{{\bullet}a}q^{\prime}
then
\underline{q}\rightarrow_{\mathtt{i}a}\underline{q^{\prime}\!}\!
.

(2)

Overhead transparency
: if
q\leadsto_{oh}q^{\prime}
then
\underline{q}=\underline{q^{\prime}}
.

(3)

Overhead termination
:
\leadsto_{oh}
terminates.

(4)

Halt
: successful states read back to
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{int}}
-normal terms, and clash states read back to clashes of
\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
.

be a final state. Two cases for

{\circ}{t}
. Then the only possibilities are that

with

with

for some

. By the closure invariant (Lemma
8.1
), this is impossible.

•

Evaluated focus

{\bullet}{v}
. Then consider the stack
S
.

–

S
is empty
. Then consider the activation stack
A
:

*

A
is empty
. Then

reads back to a value

),

) is a

-normal form.

is non-empty

\gettoappendix

thm:int-ltam-implementation

Proof.

By Proposition
F.3
, Int TAM and
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{int}}
form an implementation system on prime terms of
\lambda_{\mathtt{int}}
(because a requirement for the initial states of the Int TAM is that the term is prime), thus Int TAM implements
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{int}}
by the abstract theorem Theorem
6.3
.∎

Appendix G
Proofs and Auxiliary Notions of Sect.
9
(A Machine for
\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
: the Target TAM)

Definition G.1 (Clashes).

A state

Invariants.

The basic invariants of the Target TAM are given by the next proposition. To express the closure invariant, we need to extend the notion of norm of a term of
\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
to stacks, as follows:

\begin{array}[]{llllll}\lx@intercol\hfil\textsc{Wrapped/source norms for stacks }(\mathtt{v}\in\{\mathtt{w},\mathtt{s}\})\hfil\lx@intercol\\
\lVert S\rVert_{\mathtt{v}}&:=&\max\{i\in\mathbb{N}\,|\,\pi_{i}\mathtt{v}\mbox{ appears in $S$ out of closures bodies}\}\end{array}

Proposition G.2 (Invariants).

Let
q=(\raisebox{1.0pt}{\scalebox{0.6}{\LEFTcircle}}t\mid S\mid E\mid A)
be a Target TAM reachable state and
\mathtt{v}\in\{\mathtt{w},\mathtt{s}\}
.

(1)

Well-formedness
: all closures in
q
are well-formed, that is, such that
\lVert t\rVert_{\mathtt{w}}=\lVert b\rVert
for
{\circ}\llbracket t|b\rrbracket
or
{\bullet}\llbracket{\circ}t|{\bullet}b\rrbracket
.

(2)

Closed values
: every value
{\bullet}{v}
in
q
is closed, that is, has no projected variable out of closure bodies.

(3)

Closure
:
\lVert t\rVert_{\mathtt{v}}\leq\lVert E\rVert_{\mathtt{v}}
and
\lVert S\rVert_{\mathtt{v}}\leq\lVert E\rVert_{\mathtt{v}}
, and
\lVert S^{\prime}\rVert_{\mathtt{v}}\leq\lVert E^{\prime}\rVert_{\mathtt{v}}
for every entry
(S^{\prime},E^{\prime})
of the activation stack
A
.

Proof.

(1)

By induction on the length of the execution ending on
q
. For the initial state, it follows from the requirement that compiled terms are prime (which is an extension of well-formed). For the inductive case, one considers each transition, and the statement for the target state immediately follows from the
i.h.
about the source state.

(2)

By induction on the length of the execution ending on
q
. For each transition, it immediately follows from the
i.h.

(3)

The two parts:

(a)

\lVert t\rVert_{\mathtt{v}}\leq\lVert E\rVert_{\mathtt{v}}
and
\lVert S\rVert_{\mathtt{v}}\leq\lVert E\rVert_{\mathtt{v}}
;

(b)

\lVert S^{\prime}\rVert_{\mathtt{v}}\leq\lVert E^{\prime}\rVert_{\mathtt{v}}
for every entry
(S^{\prime},E^{\prime})
of the activation stack
A
.

are proved at the same time, by induction on the length of the execution ending on
q
. For most transitions, it immediately follows from the
i.h.
The relevant cases are (they show in particular that the two parts have to be proved simultaneously):

•

In
\leadsto_{{\circ}sub_{c}}
and
\leadsto_{{\circ}sub_{v}}
, we need the closed values invariant (Point 2) on the source state to prove part
a
about
E(p)
for the target state.

•

In
\leadsto_{{\bullet}sea_{7}}
, we need part
b
and the closed values invariant (Point 2) on the source state to prove part
a
for the target state.

•

In
\leadsto_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}
, we need part
a
on the source state to prove part
b
on the target state. Part
a
for the target state holds because of the well-formed invariant (Point 1).∎

Lemma G.4 (Read back properties).

(1)

Values
:
\underline{{\bullet}v}
is a value of
\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
for every
{\bullet}v
of the Target TAM.

(2)

Evaluation contexts
:
\underline{S}
and
\underline{A}
are evaluation contexts of
\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
for every Target TAM constructor and activation stacks
S
and
A
.

Proof.

As for the Int TAM, see the proof of Lemma
8.2
at page
F
.∎

Proposition G.5 (Target TAM/
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{int}}
implementation system).

Let
q
be a Target TAM reachable state.

(1)

Principal projection
: if
q\leadsto_{\beta_{v}}q^{\prime}
then
\underline{q}\rightarrow_{\mathtt{i}\beta_{v}}\underline{q^{\prime}}
and if
q\leadsto_{\pi}q^{\prime}
then
\underline{q}\rightarrow_{\mathtt{i}\pi}\underline{q^{\prime}}
.

(2)

Overhead transparency
: if
q\leadsto_{oh}q^{\prime}
then
\underline{q}=\underline{q^{\prime}}
.

(3)

Overhead termination
:
\leadsto_{oh}
terminates.

(4)

Halt
: successful states read back to
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{int}}
-normal terms, and clash states read back to clashes of
\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
.

Proof.

(1)

We only deal with
\leadsto_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}
, as for
\leadsto_{{\bullet}\pi}
the proof is as for the Int TAM.

\gettoappendix

thm:tar-ttam-implementation

Proof.

By Proposition
G.5
, Target TAM and
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{tar}}
form an implementation system on prime terms of
\lambda_{\mathtt{tar}}
(because a requirement for the initial states of the Target TAM is that the term is prime), thus Target TAM implements
\rightarrow_{\mathtt{tar}}
by the abstract theorem Theorem
6.3

\gettoappendix

prop:size-explosion-plotkin

Proof.

By induction on
n
. The base case
n=0
holds, because
t_{0}=\mathtt{I}=u_{0}
and
\rightarrow_{\beta_{v}}^{0}
is the
identity. The inductive case:
t_{n+1}=\pi t_{n}\rightarrow_{\beta_{v}}^{n}\pi u_{n}=(\lambda x.\lambda y.yxx)u_{n}\rightarrow_{\beta_{v}}\lambda y.yu_{n}u_{n}=u_{n+1}
, where the first sequence
is obtained by the
i.h.
, and the last step by the fact that
u_{n}
is a value by
i.h.
The bounds on the
sizes are immediate, as well as the fact that
u_{n+1}
is a value.
∎

\gettoappendix

l:TAM-sub-term-invariant

Proof.

By induction on the length
|r|
of the execution
r\colon t^{\circ}\leadsto_{\textup{\tiny STAM}}^{*}q
.
If
|r|=0
then the statement trivially holds, since
q=t^{\circ}=({\circ}(t,\epsilon)\mid\epsilon)
.

Otherwise
r\colon t^{\circ}\leadsto_{\textup{\tiny STAM}}^{*}q
is the concatenation of
r^{\prime}\colon t^{\circ}\leadsto_{\textup{\tiny STAM}}^{*}q^{\prime}
and
q^{\prime}\leadsto_{\textup{\tiny STAM}}q
.
By
i.h.
, the statement holds for
r^{\prime}
. A straightforward analysis of the transition rules of the machine proves that the statement is preserved by the transition
q^{\prime}\leadsto_{\textup{\tiny STAM}}q
.
∎

in the stack), thus

. ∎

\gettoappendix

prop:TAM-number-of-trans

Proof.

First, we prove
|q|_{oh}\leq|t^{\circ}|_{oh}+|r|_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}\cdot|t|-|r|_{{\circ}sub,{\circ}sea_{1-5},{\bullet}sea_{6}}
, and then we deduce the statement. The proof is by induction on the length
|r|
of
r
. If
r
is empty then the inequality becomes
|q|_{oh}=|t^{\circ}|_{oh}\leq|t^{\circ}|_{oh}
, which is true. If
r
is non-empty then one considers the last transitions of
r
, that is, let
r^{\prime}:t^{\circ}\leadsto_{\textup{\tiny STAM}}^{|r|-1}q^{\prime}
be
r
without its last transition
q^{\prime}\leadsto_{\textup{\tiny STAM}}q
. By
i.h.
,
|q|_{oh}\leq|t^{\circ}|_{oh}+|r^{\prime}|_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}\cdot|t|-|r^{\prime}|_{{\circ}sub,{\circ}sea_{1-5},{\bullet}sea_{6}}
. Case of this last transition:

•

\leadsto_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}
: by Lemma
11.3
.1, the left-hand side of the inequality grows of at most
|t|
, which is also the increase of the right-hand side.

•

\leadsto_{{\circ}sub,{\circ}sea_{1-5},{\bullet}sea_{6}}
: by Lemma
11.3
.2, the left-hand side of the inequality decreases of at least
1
, and the right-hand side decreases of 1.

•

\leadsto_{{\bullet}\pi,{\bullet}sea_{1-3}}
: by Lemma
11.3
.3, both the left-hand and the right-hand side of the inequality do not change.

Thus, we proved the inequality. It follows that
|r|_{{\circ}sub,{\circ}sea_{1-5},{\bullet}sea_{6}}\leq|t^{\circ}|_{oh}+|r|_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}\cdot|t|
. By definition,
|t^{\circ}|_{oh}=|{\circ}(t,\epsilon)|_{oh}=|t|
. Then,

|t^{\circ}|_{oh}+|r|_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}\cdot|t|\ \ \leq\ \ |t|+|r|_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}\cdot|t|\ \ =\ \ (|r|_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}+1)\cdot|t|.

Summing up, the inequality is:

|r|_{{\circ}sub,{\circ}sea_{1-5},{\bullet}sea_{6}}\leq(|r|_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}+1)\cdot|t|

Now, we finally obtain our bound of
|r|
by applying twice the derived inequality:

\begin{array}[]{llll}|r|&=&|r|_{{\circ}sub,{\circ}sea_{1-5}}+|r|_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}+|r|_{{\bullet}\pi,{\bullet}sea_{1,3,6}}\\
&\leq_{{L.\ref{l:TAM-blue-bound}}}&|r|_{{\circ}sub,{\circ}sea_{1-5}}+|r|_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}+|r|_{{\circ}sea_{1-3},{\bullet}sea_{6}}\\
&\leq&|r|_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}+2\cdot(|r|_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}+1)\cdot|t|\\
&\leq&3\cdot(|r|_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}+1)\cdot|t|\end{array}

Where the last inequality is justified by the fact that
|t|\geq 1
.
∎

Number of (Overhead) Transitions

We follow the schema used for the Source TAM. The new transition
\leadsto_{{\bullet}sea_{7}}
is part of the transitions that are factored out, since each
\leadsto_{{\bullet}sea_{7}}
transition is enabled by a
\leadsto_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}
transition adding an entry to the activation stack.

Lemma J.1 (Transitions match).

Let
r\colon q\leadsto_{\textup{\tiny TTAM}}^{*}q^{\prime}
be an execution. Then
|r|_{\pi,{\bullet}sea_{1,3,7}}\leq|r|_{{\circ}sea_{1,2,3},{\bullet}\beta_{v}}
.

Proof.

Every transition
\leadsto_{{\bullet}sea_{1}}
in
r
must be preceded by a transition
\leadsto_{{\circ}sea_{1}}
(otherwise there would not be an entry of shape
{\circ}u
in the constructor stack), thus
|r|_{{\bullet}sea_{1}}\leq|r|_{{\circ}sea_{1}}
.

Every transition
\leadsto_{{\bullet}sea_{3}}
in
r
must be preceded by a transition
\leadsto_{{\circ}sea_{3}}
(otherwise there would not be an entry of shape
\llparenthesis\downarrow,\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.}\rrparenthesis
in the constructor stack), thus
|r|_{{\bullet}sea_{3}}\leq|r|_{{\circ}sea_{3}}
.

Every transition
\leadsto_{{\bullet}\pi}
in
r
must be preceded by a transition
\leadsto_{{\circ}sea_{2}}
(otherwise there would not be an entry of shape
\pi_{i}
in the constructor stack), thus
|r|_{\pi}\leq|r|_{{\circ}sea_{2}}
.

Every transition
\leadsto_{{\bullet}sea_{7}}
in
r
must be preceded by a transition
\leadsto_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}
(otherwise there would not be an entry on the activation stack), thus
|r|_{{\bullet}sea_{7}}\leq|r|_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}
. ∎

14
. It is a direct adaptation to the Target TAM of the measure given for the Source TAM (see Fig.

, page

of the paper). Note indeed that the measure ignores environments, which are the main difference between the two machines.

\gettoappendix

prop:LTAM-number-of-trans

Proof.

The proof is essentially as for the Source TAM. We detail it anyway.
First, we prove
|q|_{oh}\leq|t^{\circ}|_{oh}+|r|_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}\cdot|t|-|r|_{{\circ}sub_{c},{\circ}sub_{v},{\circ}sea_{1-5},{\bullet}sea_{6}}
, and then we deduce the statement. The proof is by induction on the length
|r|
of
r
. If
r
is empty then the inequality becomes
|q|_{oh}=|t^{\circ}|_{oh}\leq|t^{\circ}|_{oh}
, which is true. If
r
is non-empty then one considers the last transitions of
r
, that is, let
r^{\prime}:t^{\circ}\leadsto_{\textup{\tiny TTAM}}^{|r|-1}q^{\prime}
be
r
without its last transition
q^{\prime}\leadsto_{\textup{\tiny TTAM}}q
. By
i.h.
,
|q|_{oh}\leq|t^{\circ}|_{oh}+|r^{\prime}|_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}\cdot|t|-|r^{\prime}|_{{\circ}sub_{c},{\circ}sub_{v},{\circ}sea_{1-5},{\bullet}sea_{6}}
. Case of this last transition:

•

\leadsto_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}
: by Lemma
J.2
.1, the left-hand side of the inequality grows of at most
|t|
, which is also the increase of the right-hand side.

•

\leadsto_{{\circ}sub_{c},{\circ}sub_{v},{\circ}sea_{1-5},{\bullet}sea_{6}}
: by Lemma
J.2
.2, the left-hand side of the inequality decreases of at least
1
, and the right-hand side decreases of 1.

•

\leadsto_{{\bullet}\pi,{\bullet}sea_{1,3,7}}
: by Lemma
J.2
.3, both the left-hand and the right-hand side of the inequality do not change.

Thus, we proved the inequality. It follows that
|r|_{{\circ}sub_{c},{\circ}sub_{v},{\circ}sea_{1-5},{\bullet}sea_{6}}\leq|t^{\circ}|_{oh}+|r|_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}\cdot|t|
. By definition,
|t^{\circ}|_{oh}=|({\circ}t\mid\epsilon\mid\epsilon\mid\epsilon)|_{oh}=|t|
. Then,

|t^{\circ}|_{oh}+|r|_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}\cdot|t|\ \ \leq\ \ |t|+|r|_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}\cdot|t|\ \ =\ \ (|r|_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}+1)\cdot|t|.

Summing up, the inequality is:

|r|_{{\circ}sub_{c},{\circ}sub_{v},{\circ}sea_{1-5},{\bullet}sea_{6}}\leq(|r|_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}+1)\cdot|t|

Now, we finally obtain our bound of
|r|
by applying twice the derived inequality:

\begin{array}[]{llll}|r|&=&|r|_{{\circ}sub_{c},{\circ}sub_{v},{\circ}sea_{1-5}}+|r|_{{\bullet}\beta}+|r|_{{\bullet}\pi,{\bullet}sea_{1,3,6}}\\
&\leq_{{L.\ref{l:LTAM-blue-bound}}}&|r|_{{\circ}sub_{c},{\circ}sub_{v},{\circ}sea_{1-5}}+|r|_{{\bullet}\beta}+|r|_{{\circ}sea_{1-3},{\bullet}sea_{6}}\\
&\leq&|r|_{{\bullet}\beta}+2\cdot(|r|_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}+1)\cdot|t|\\
&\leq&3\cdot(|r|_{{\bullet}\beta_{v}}+1)\cdot|t|\end{array}

Where the last inequality is justified by the fact that
|t|\geq 1
.
∎

\gettoappendix

l:lifting-growth-bound

Proof.

Point 1: the size increment in
\underline{t}
is due to the bags introduced by wrapping abstractions, and it is proportional to the number of free variables in the body of the abstraction, bounded by
\mathtt{hg}(t)
; so
|\underline{t}|\in{\mathcal{O}}(\mathtt{hg}(t)\cdot|t|)
.
Point 2: take
t_{n}:=\lambda x_{1}.\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.}\lambda x_{n}.x_{1}x_{2}\ldots x_{n}\allowbreak\neq\lambda x_{1},\hbox to6.00006pt{.\hss.},x_{n}.x_{1}x_{2}\ldots x_{n}
(note
n
abstractions in
t_{n}
, not just
1
).
∎

Appendix K
Implementation in OCaml of the Target TAM

The submission comes with an implementation in OCaml of the Target TAM,
available on GitHub
(
Sacerdoti Coen 2025
)
.

Motivations

The aims of the implementation are:

(1)

Supporting the claim that all Target TAM transitions can be
implemented in constant time, with the exception of
\leadsto_{{\circ}sea_{3}}
and
\leadsto_{{\circ}sub_{c}}
whose complexity is linear in the width of the
tuple/bag iterated over by the rule (in the paper
\leadsto_{{\circ}sea_{3}}
and
\leadsto_{{\circ}sub_{c}}
are then considered
{\mathcal{O}}(1)
operations because the linear cost is amortized over the cost of search in complete machine runs);

(2)

Giving the user the possibility of observing Target TAM executions on terms of their own
choice, to better grasp the way the machine works.

The implementation is
not
meant to be optimized, nor to represent
an instance of state-of-the-art OCaml code. In particular, the data
structures have been chosen to make the datatypes and code very close
to those in the paper, to allow the reader to verify that the
implementation reflects its specification.

User Interface and Provided Examples

Once compiled following the instructions in
the
README.md
file, the user can start a Read-Eval-Print-Loop
(REPL) by typing
dune exec main
. The loop requires the user to
enter a source term, which is then

(1)

Wrapped to intermediate code,

(2)

Turned into target code by eliminating names, and then

(3)

Run according to the transitions of the Target TAM.

Every intermediate machine transition is printed on the standard output.
The internal representation of the parsed source and intermediate terms
are also printed before starting reduction.

The exact syntax accepted by the REPL is printed when the command is run.
It is the user responsibility to enter closed and clash-free terms.
When one of the latter two conditions is violated, the REPL will abort.

The
TESTS
file includes a few examples of closed, clash-free
source terms that can be used as tests by typing them at the REPL prompt
or by feeding the whole file to the executable via
dune exec main < TESTS
.

Code Structure

The code consists of the following files:

•

lexer.mll/parser.mly
where the lexer and parser for
source terms are implemented

•

term.ml
composed of three sub-modules

Source/Intermediate/Target
respectively for the source,
intermediate and target languages. Each submodule defined the
algebraic type
term
for the terms of the language.
The wrapping and name elimination functions to turn source terms
into intermediate terms and intermediate terms into target terms
are implemented in the sub-modules of the function codomain.

Note that, in the memory model of OCaml, every subterm is represented
in memory as a pointer to its root. Therefore pattern matching over
a term and calling a function on the pattern variables that hold
the subterms is done in constant time. This is required to conclude
that the implementation of most machine transitions requires constant
time.

•

machine.ml
where the Target TAM is implemented.
The module begins with the definition of
algebraic data types for constructor and activation stacks,
environments and states of a machine. Then a pretty-printing sub-module
PP
allows to turn all of
the previous types to string. The code is not written with efficiency
in mind. The functions are parameterized by a boolean stating if the
term has already been evaluated or not. The boolean is propagated
during recursion according to the machine invariants and it is used
to decorate every subterm with
{\circ}/{\bullet}
.
Outside the
PP
sub-module, the last two functions of the file
are
run
, which implements the machine transitions and main
loop, and
reduce
, that builds an initial machine state from
a target term, computes its normal form using
run
and
prints it.

Differences Between the Code and the Paper

The definitions
in the paper and the code are almost in one-to-one correspondence.
There is no distinction in the code between values and terms.
Arrays are used to represent bags and tuples and to provide access in
constant time.

The only significant difference is in the stack entry
for tuples under evaluation
\llparenthesis\widetilde{\hbox{${\circ}t$}},\downarrow,\widetilde{\hbox{${\bullet}v$}}\rrparenthesis
that is represented in the code as the array of terms

\widetilde{\hbox{${\circ}t$}}u\widetilde{\hbox{${\bullet}v$}}
together with the index
i

of
\downarrow
, so that the
i
-th element of the array is
a non-meaningful term
u
that replaces the
\downarrow

placeholder. This choice allows us to use arrays of terms both for tuples
and for stack entries, simplifying the implementation in two ways:
it allows us to do a shallow copy of the tuple in input in the

\leadsto_{{\circ}sea_{3}}
transition, to obtain the needed stack item;
it also allows us to avoid a shallow copy of the array in the

\leadsto_{{\bullet}sea_{3}}
and
\leadsto_{{\bullet}sea_{3}}
rules.
